title: How to Lead Without Letting Instinct Lead You
author: Andrea Chiarelli et al.
summary: The essay argues that under pressure leaders regress to primal instincts, which it dramatizes with corporate animal archetypes such as the snake, lion, scorpion, peacock and shark. These instincts are not flaws in themselves, but they become destructive once they turn into default behaviour, and power makes the drift easier because fewer people challenge the leader. The authors answer with a three-step pause, channel, choose sequence that is meant to hand control back from the amygdala to the prefrontal cortex. They illustrate it with a CEO who meets a missed quarter by steering the room toward process, people and external factors instead of interrogation. The move is to treat leadership as mastery over instinct rather than its absence, and to build in outside checks such as a trusted peer who names your animal privately. It is a short, practical piece on emotional self-regulation for leaders, framed more by metaphor than by evidence.
points: Under stress the brain reacts before it reasons, so a leader's first impulse (interrupting, withdrawing, watching) is often a survival habit rather than a considered choice.
Each archetype's strength becomes its liability when it is the default, for example the shark who delivers results but leaves fear and lost trust behind.
Seniority raises the risk because the higher a leader climbs the less they are challenged, making it easy to rationalise instinct as standard behaviour.
The prescribed practice is Pause, Channel, Choose: notice the body signals, ask what the instinct is protecting, then pick the response the moment needs.
Naming your personal trigger zones and recruiting a trusted peer to flag hijacked judgment in private makes self-awareness durable.
quotes: Corporate power doesn’t roar. It slithers, stalks or waits. Walk into any boardroom and you can feel it before anyone speaks—the stillness before someone asserts control, the way a single interruption can redraw the hierarchy.
However, leadership, unlike survival, isn’t about winning a single fight. It’s about sustaining trust. And that means knowing when instinct helps you lead and when it undermines you.
Power amplifies this drift: the higher you climb, the less you’re challenged, and the easier it is to rationalise instinct as standard behaviour.
Understanding this is an act of self-preservation. When you can recognise your own pattern under stress, you regain choice. And choice is the purest form of leadership control there is.

We also recommend that you find a trusted peer who can call you out gently when your instincts hijack your judgment. Ideally, you should do this in private (as opposed to during meetings or live conversations), so you can digest the feedback without spiralling into defence mode.

The paradox of modern leadership is that the more chaotic the environment becomes, the more people look for calm. And leadership isn’t the absence of the predator or pretending we are immune to instinct.
